extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/graduate students and researchers in combinatorics, graph theory, and combinatorial geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Collection of classical theorems, definitions, and proof techniques in combinatorics, graph theory, planar graphs, and combinatorial geometry (Erdős–de Bruijn, Graham–Pollak, slope problem, Euler's formula, Sylvester–Gallai, Pick's theorem, Cauchy rigidity, etc.). Includes statements, combinatorial/linear-algebraic proofs, and illustrative examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erdős–de Bruijn theorem (set-system formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let A1,...,Am be proper subsets of X (|X| = n) such that every pair of elements of X is contained in precisely one set Ai. Then m > n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two proofs are given: a direct combinatorial counting using r_x (number of Ai containing x) that leads to a contradiction if m <= n, and a short linear-algebra proof using the incidence matrix B (rows indexed by X, columns by Ai). For the linear-algebra proof consider B B^T: off-diagonals are 1, diagonal entries are r_x; B B^T is positive definite (invertible) so rank(B) >= n, implying m >= n+1 (i.e., m > n). The theorem is presented together with the equivalent graph formulation: a decomposition of the complete graph K_n into m cliques (all different from K_n) with every edge in a unique clique forces m > n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graph formulation of Erdős–de Bruijn (clique decomposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: If we decompose the complete graph K_n into m cliques, different from K_n, so that every edge is in a unique clique, then m > n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the direct translation of the set-system theorem: take vertex set X as vertices of K_n and Ai as vertex sets of the cliques. The same linear-algebra or combinatorial arguments apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham–Pollak theorem (decomposition into complete bipartite graphs)
rubrics_metrics.description: If K_n is decomposed into m complete bipartite subgraphs, then m > n - 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No known purely combinatorial proof; proofs use linear algebra. One proof (Tverberg) assigns variables x_i to vertices 1..n and uses the incidence between parts L_j, R_j of each bipartite subgraph H_j to obtain linear equations sum_{i in L_j} x_i = sum_{i in R_j} x_i for j=1..m. If m < n-1 then the homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution, which leads to a contradiction when plugged back into the decomposition identity. Example decomposition by stars shows n-1 is attainable, and the theorem shows optimality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic graph definitions and conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: A graph G = (V,E) where V is a finite vertex set and E a finite set of edges connecting pairs of vertices. Consider simple graphs (no loops, no multiple edges) unless stated otherwise. Definitions of adjacency/neighbor, incidence (vertex-edge), subgraph, induced subgraph, isomorphism, connectedness, clique, independent set, forest, tree, bipartite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These standard definitions are used throughout. Remarks include that isomorphism preserves incidences, induced subgraphs contain every edge between chosen vertices, trees are connected acyclic graphs, and bipartite graphs are isomorphic to subgraphs of complete bipartite graphs (vertex partition into two independent sets). Examples: K_n, K_{m,n}, paths P_n. The section also notes complexity questions (graph isomorphism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Slope problem theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: If n >= 3 points in the plane do not lie on one single line, then they determine at least n - 1 different slopes; equality is possible only if n is odd and n >= 5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof reduces the geometric problem to a combinatorial model (Goodman–Pollack) of a periodic sequence of permutations obtained by projecting points in a rotating direction. Key properties of the sequence: starts at 1..n, ends at n..1, length t equals number of slopes, each pair i<j is switched exactly once, and each move reverses one or more disjoint increasing substrings. Analyze crossing/touching/ordinary moves relative to a central barrier splitting permutations into left/right halves; count letters crossing the barrier and use inequalities (facts about numbers of ordinary moves between crossing and touching moves) to deduce t > n for even n, finishing by a reduction for odd n. Examples and small sequences are given; reference to constructions showing sharpness for odd n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goodman–Pollack combinatorial model (permutation-sequence reduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Model a planar point configuration by a periodic sequence of permutations obtained by projecting on a rotating line; the sequence has properties: starts at 123...n, ends at n...321, every pair is switched exactly once, length equals number of slopes, and each move reverses disjoint increasing substrings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduction is central to solving the slope problem. The text lists properties used in the counting argument and illustrates with small examples. It explains how moves correspond to passing a direction over one or more configuration slopes and how reversal of increasing substrings captures the combinatorics of the projection order changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Move taxonomy in permutation model: crossing, touching, ordinary (and counting orders)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moves in the permutation sequence are classified: a crossing move reverses a substring that crosses the central barrier and moves 2d letters across (order d); a touching move reverses a substring adjacent to the barrier (does not cross); ordinary moves are neither. Each letter must cross the barrier at least once; orders d_i of crossing moves satisfy sum 2 d_i >= 2n. Additional facts: between any two crossing moves there's at least one touching move; between a crossing move of order d and the next touching move there are at least d-1 ordinary moves (and a symmetric statement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These combinatorial constraints on the T/C/O pattern imply lower bounds on the total sequence length t (via embedding crossing moves into T-0-C patterns of length 2d), which yields the slope bound. The reasoning is illustrated with examples showing counting of letters and move types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euler's formula for connected plane graphs
rubrics_metrics.description: If G is a connected plane graph with n vertices, e edges, and f faces, then n - e + f = 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof given using a spanning tree T in G and the dual graph G*: edges E\T correspond to a spanning tree T* in G*. For trees v = e + 1; applying to T and T* and adding yields n + f = e + 2. The exposition emphasizes the constructive duality and uses the formula to derive further numerical consequences and classical results (e.g., Platonic solids classification, nonplanarity of K5 and K3,3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of Euler's formula: K5 and K3,3 nonplanarity and platonic solids
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications: using n, e values and average face-side counts derived from Euler's formula one deduces K5 and K3,3 are nonplanar and obtains restrictions that lead to classification of the Platonic solids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example computations: for K5, n=5, e=10 -> f=7 gives average face-sides < 3, impossible; for K3,3, n=6, e=9 -> f=5 gives average face-sides < 4, contradicting bipartiteness (cycles length >=4). The method is double-counting edges by face-sides and using average inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local consequences of Euler's formula (Proposition: A,B,C)
rubrics_metrics.description: (A) Any simple plane graph with n>2 has a vertex of degree at most 5. (B) Such a graph has at most 3n - 6 edges. (C) If the edges are two-colored, there is a vertex with at most two color-changes in the cyclic order of incident edges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs use double-counting face-sides and degrees: (A) assume all degrees >=6 and derive contradiction with Euler by inequalities 2e - 3f > 0 and 2e - 6n > 0; (B) follows similarly to get e <= 3n - 6; (C) counts corners with color changes and bounds them by face-side counts to reach a contradiction if every vertex has >=4 changes, hence proving existence of a vertex with <=2 changes. These local statements are then used as tools in later theorems (Sylvester–Gallai, monochromatic lines, Cauchy's theorem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sylvester–Gallai theorem (via Euler)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given any set of n > 3 points in the plane, not all collinear, there is always a line that contains exactly two of the points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by lifting to the unit sphere, replacing point pairs by antipodal pairs and dualizing to great circles. The intersection arrangement of great circles gives a simple plane graph on S^2 with all vertex degrees even and >=4; by proposition (A) there is a vertex of degree 4, i.e., a great circle intersection incident to exactly two great circles, corresponding back to a line containing exactly two original points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monochromatic lines theorem (Don Chakerian)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given any finite configuration of black and white points in the plane, not all collinear, there exists a monochromatic line (a line containing at least two points of one color and none of the other).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Again lift to the sphere and dualize to colored great circles. Use part (C) of the Proposition: at a vertex where great circles of different colors intersect there are at least 4 corners with sign changes, implying existence of an intersection lying only on great circles of one color (a monochromatic intersection point), which corresponds to a monochromatic line in the plane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pick's theorem (lattice polygon area formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any polygon Q in R^2 with integral vertices, area A(Q) = n_int + n_bd / 2 - 1, where n_int is number of interior lattice points and n_bd number of lattice points on the boundary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: triangulate Q using all interior and boundary lattice points; elementary triangles (triangles with integral vertices and no other lattice points) have area 1/2 (proved via lattice-basis/determinant argument). Count triangles (f - 1) and relate number of edges and vertices via double counting and Euler's formula to obtain the area formula. Example and lemma about elementary triangles included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy's rigidity theorem (convex polyhedra)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two 3-dimensional convex polyhedra P and P' are combinatorially equivalent with corresponding facets congruent, then the dihedral angles between corresponding pairs of adjacent facets are equal; hence P and P' are congruent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof (Cauchy): color an edge black if the corresponding dihedral angle in P' is larger, white if smaller. Project the colored edge graph radially to the sphere; by Proposition (C) there is a vertex with at most two color-changes. Intersect small spheres around such a vertex to get convex (spherical) polygons Q and Q' with corresponding side lengths equal; mark + for angles opened and - for closed. Using Cauchy's arm lemma (next entry) one derives contradictions (if only one sign) or contradictions via a separation line (if both signs), forcing all dihedral angles equal. Remarks: convexity is essential; nonconvex counterexamples exist (Connelly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy's arm lemma (polygonal edge-length/angle inequality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let Q and Q' be convex planar or spherical n-gons with corresponding side lengths equal except possibly the 'missing' final edge, and suppose interior angles satisfy a_i < a'_i for 2 <= i <= n-1. Then the length of the missing edge in Q is strictly less than that in Q', with equality iff all a_i = a'_i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by induction on n: base n=3 follows from the cosine rule (planar or spherical). For n>4, either cut off a vertex where angles equal and apply induction, or produce a modified convex polygon Q* by enlarging one angle to keep convexity and then compare Q*, Q' by induction and triangle inequality to deduce the strict inequality. The lemma underpins the final contradiction in the Cauchy rigidity proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remarks on flexibility and the bellows conjecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Convexity is essential for Cauchy's theorem; there exist non-convex triangulated spheres embedded in R^3 that are flexible (Connelly). Recent work (Connelly, Sabitov & Walz) proved that the volume enclosed by any such flexible surface remains constant (bellows conjecture).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are historical and contextual notes: Connelly's 1977 counterexamples show continuous deformations keeping faces congruent for nonconvex triangulated spheres. Subsequent results show invariance of enclosed volume under flexing. References are provided.
